e.etymology: A short form of Burton, an English surname from places named 'fortified settlement' (Old English burh and tun), and a spelling of Bert, short for Albert and Herbert, from Germanic beraht, 'bright'.

assoc.t: Burt's Bees, lip balm and skin care brand

e.etymology: A respelling of Shannon, from the River Shannon in Ireland. Its Irish name, Sionainn, is linked to Old Irish sen, 'old' or 'wise', and in legend to the goddess Sionann.
An African American name of the 1970s built with the Ta- prefix, in a family with Tawanna and Tawanda; the ending echoes Wanda and Juana.
A phonetic spelling of Janine, the French pet form of Jeanne, the feminine of Jean (John). It goes back to Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
A form of Teresa or Therese, a name first recorded in Spain and often linked to Greek therizo, 'to harvest', or the island of Thera. Terese is also the usual Swedish and Norwegian spelling.
A respelling of Vicky, the short form of Victoria, which is the Latin word for victory and the name of the Roman goddess of victory.
A respelling of Jamie, the Scottish pet form of James, which comes through Latin from Hebrew Ya'aqov (Jacob), traditionally explained as 'holder of the heel' or 'supplanter'.
e.note: Reads like jammies, the children's word for pajamas, and is often said JAM-ee on first sight.

e.etymology: A spelling of Blanche, from Old French blanc, 'white', first a nickname for a fair-haired or pale woman. It came to England with the Normans.
e.note: Blanch is also an English verb: to turn pale, or to boil vegetables briefly.

e.etymology: A spelling of Latasha, an African American name of the 1970s that puts the La- prefix on Tasha, the short form of Natasha (Russian, from Latin natalis, 'Christmas Day').
An African American name of the 1970s and 80s that joins the La- prefix to the -quita ending of Marquita and Chiquita.
The French form of Hortensia, the feminine of the Roman family name Hortensius, from Latin hortus, 'garden'. Hortensia is also the French and Spanish word for the hydrangea.
A pet name from the 19th-century American South, used mostly for Martha and sometimes for Matilda or Mehitabel. Theodore Roosevelt's mother, Martha Bulloch, was known as Mittie.
A spelling of Nanette, a French pet form of Anne, which comes from Hebrew Channah, 'grace' or 'favor'.
An elaboration of Pearl with the -ine ending, popular in the American South in the early 1900s. Pearl is the English word for the gem, from Old French perle.
A surname with two sources: Norman d'Orsay, 'from Orsay' in France, and Irish O Dorchaidhe, 'descendant of the dark one'. It was a boys' first name in the US in the early 1900s.
From Spanish chiquita, 'little girl', the feminine diminutive of chico, 'small'. It became a given name in the US in the 1970s and 80s.
An African American name of the 1970s and 80s, built from the Sha- prefix and the -meka sound of Tameka and Tamika.
From Greek myrtos, 'myrtle'; Myrtis of Anthedon was an ancient Greek poet. In the American South it was used in the early 1900s as a dressier form of Myrtle.
In the US it rose in the 1970s as a spelling of Shanda and a relative of Chandra. Chanda is also an Indian name: Sanskrit chanda means 'fierce', and in Hindi chanda is a fond word for the moon.
An English surname from Old French gaillard, 'lively, high-spirited', brought over by the Normans. It was a fairly common American boys' name in the early 1900s.
namesakes: Gaylord Focker (Ben Stiller's character in Meet the Parents)

assoc.t: Gaylord Hotels, including Gaylord Opryland in Nashville

e.note: Draws teasing because it starts with gay; the joke runs through Meet the Parents, where Greg Focker's real name is Gaylord.

e.etymology: A spelling of Letha, which is probably a short form of Aletha, from Greek aletheia, 'truth'. Some connect it instead to Lethe, the river of forgetfulness in Greek myth.
A respelling of Brittany, the English name of the region of northwest France settled by Britons in the 5th century. Brittany became a popular American girls' name in the 1980s.
A respelling of Craig, a Scottish surname for someone who lived near a crag, from Gaelic creag, 'rock'.
A respelling of Vicky, the short form of Victoria, which is the Latin word for victory and the name of the Roman goddess of victory.
Probably a blend of Leah and Beatrice. Silent film star Leatrice Joy made it known in the 1920s, when it had its peak in the US.
An English-sounding stand-in for Chaim, from Hebrew chayyim, 'life'. Jewish immigrants in the US adopted it widely in the early 1900s.
namesakes: Hyman Rickover (admiral, father of the nuclear navy)
Hyman Roth (mob boss in The Godfather Part II)
e.note: Sounds the same as hymen, the anatomical term, which invites teasing.

assoc.t: sounds the same as hymen, the anatomical membrane

e.etymology: An African American name of the 1970s that adds the -da ending of Rhonda and Lashonda to Sharon.
The French form of Norman, 'Northman', the name given to the Vikings who settled Normandy. French Canadian families brought it to New England.
A spelling of Gay, from the English word in its older sense of merry or carefree (Old French gai). It was used as a girls' name through the mid-1900s.

assoc.t: sounds the same as gay, the word for homosexual

e.note: Said exactly like gay; the name fell out of use as the word came to mean homosexual.

e.etymology: A respelling of Tina, a short form of Christina, Martina and other names ending in -tina that became a name of its own.
A variant of Hobart, itself an English surname form of Hubert, from Germanic hug, 'mind, heart', and beraht, 'bright'.
